meta.title: AI Is Rewriting the Operating System of Pathology

glossary.definition: A model that is given tools and a goal rather than a single prompt: it plans, calls the tools, reads what comes back, and decides what to do next. In 2025–26 pathology agents navigate whole-slide images, run analysis code, and cite the regions they used.

A packaging convention (Anthropic, October 2025; open standard December 2025) for giving an agent a reusable, inspectable procedure — instructions plus any scripts and resources it needs — instead of re-explaining the procedure in every prompt.
Vannevar Bush's 1945 term for a named, re-traversable path linking one document to another. The memex stored trails; the point was that the linking, not the storage, was the intellectual act.
A learned weighting that decides how much each tile contributes to a slide-level prediction. ABMIL spreads weight almost evenly; CHIEF concentrates it, which is what makes it useful as a router.

Area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve — the probability that a random positive case is ranked above a random negative one. It measures discrimination only: it says nothing about calibration, about the decision threshold, or about whether using the model changes anything.

Systematic signal that tracks how or where data were produced rather than what they contain. In pathology this is scanner, stain, and site: in ten public foundation models, the medical center of origin is predicted more accurately than the tissue type.
The point at which the leading entries on a benchmark are no longer statistically distinguishable, so the benchmark stops being able to rank them and the interesting variance moves elsewhere.
Resampling the evaluation set with replacement — 1,000 times, in the Stanford benchmark — to put a confidence interval around a performance estimate.

Whether a model's stated probability matches the observed frequency. A model can discriminate well (high AUROC) and still be badly calibrated, which is what matters the moment a number is used to make a decision.
A pathology foundation model (Wang et al., Nature 2024; 60,530 WSIs) whose attention weights are used inside EAGLE as a frozen ranker — the cheap step that decides where the expensive model looks.
A vision–language pathology foundation model (Lu et al., Nat Med 2024). CONCH v1.5 appears in EAGLE's comparison at 191.85 seconds per slide.

An adapter that exposes an institutional system — a repository, a database, a scanner archive — to a model as a callable tool. Claude for Life Sciences shipped connectors for Benchling, PubMed and others in October 2025; there is still no pathology or WSI connector.

Deciding what an agent should have in front of it at each step: which files, which prior results, which instructions, and what to leave out. It has quietly replaced prompt wording as the thing that determines whether an agent works.
A 2022 transformer-based tile encoder, used inside EAGLE for the cheap first pass over every tile at 2 microns per pixel.
A structured description of a dataset — how it was collected, who is in it, what it should not be used for. The dataset analogue of a model card.
An analysis of net clinical benefit across the range of thresholds a clinician might actually use. Neither anchor paper reports one; almost no computational-pathology paper does.
The whole-slide-imaging extension to DICOM. Final text 2010 — the standard is sixteen years old, and the 2025 Connectathon still counted only 32 implementers.

Efficient Approach for Guided Local Examination — the Kather-lab framework (Nat Commun, 1 July 2026) in which a frozen CHIEF ranker selects 25 tiles out of roughly 18,000 for an expensive encoder to re-read.
A fixed-length vector standing in for an image, a tile, or a slide. EAGLE's output is a single 1,280-dimensional vector per slide — small enough to store, reuse, and search.
The four distinct claims this lecture keeps apart: I saw it work · I reproduced it · it is deployed in a workflow · it improved something for a patient. Each requires a different kind of evidence.
Evaluating on cohorts that contributed nothing to training or model selection. Internal cross-validation on additional tasks is not external validation, however many tasks it adds.

The 1828–1848 canal from New Haven to Northampton, chartered under Yale treasurer James Hillhouse. It cost more than a million dollars, turned a profit once in its first decade, and was closed and railed over on its own right-of-way.

A large model pre-trained on unlabeled data and then reused, usually frozen, as a feature extractor for many downstream tasks. In pathology the 2024 cohort — UNI, CONCH, Prov-GigaPath, CHIEF, Virchow2 — is what every 2026 benchmark is comparing.

Using a pre-trained model's outputs without updating its weights. Both anchor papers evaluate frozen features, which makes them comparable and also makes them a lower bound on what a fine-tuned model could do.

A model whose weights require accepting terms and receiving approval before download. Virchow2 is gated; CHIEF's weights are requested separately. Reproducing a published result can therefore require three separate permissions.
Integrated Biospecimen and Informatics System — a natural-language search layer over pathology data built at Yale so that a cohort question can be asked without writing a query.
The IHE Pathology and Laboratory Medicine Digital Pathology Workflow – Image Acquisition profile. Revision 1.3, December 2024, still Trial Implementation.

The regulatory statement of what a device is for, in whom, and by whom. Performance is only meaningful relative to it; a model with excellent AUROC and no intended use has not made a clinical claim at all.
The public log of a repository's bugs and unmet expectations. It is the only artifact in the whole ecosystem whose primary function is to reveal failure modes.

In vitro diagnostic. Pathology AI in the United States is generally reviewed as an IVD component under OHT7, not as software-as-a-medical-device — which is why the FDA's AI device list shows nine pathology entries and 1,164 radiology ones.

Freezing a model and training only a single linear layer on top. It measures how much task-relevant information the representation already contains, and it deliberately excludes everything fine-tuning could add.
Laboratory Information System — specimen tracking, result reporting, quality control. It carries every case in the building and will keep doing so; that is the canal, not an insult.
Knuth's 1984 proposal that a program should be written as an explanation to a human being, with the executable code embedded in the prose rather than the other way round.

Model Context Protocol — an open standard (Anthropic, November 2024; donated to the Linux Foundation in December 2025) for connecting models to tools and data sources through one interface instead of one integration per pair.
Averaging tile-level features into a slide-level feature. Simple, reproducible, and — as the Stanford benchmark notes among its own limitations — almost certainly leaving performance on the table.
The desk-sized machine Bush described in 1945: it stores what you read, and above all it lets you build and consult trails between items. Every idea in this lecture's last act is a footnote to it.
Multiple-instance learning — training on bags of tiles with only a slide-level label, because nobody annotated eighteen thousand tiles.
A short structured document stating what a model was trained on, what it is for, how it was evaluated, and where it should not be used (Mitchell et al., 2019).

Microns per pixel — the resolution a slide is read at. EAGLE tessellates at 0.5 MPP and runs its cheap pass at 2 MPP, which is why the same slide is about 18,000 tiles in one sentence and about 1,100 in the next.
Predetermined Change Control Plan — the FDA mechanism that lets an authorized AI device be updated along a pre-agreed path without a new submission.
A whole-slide foundation model trained on 1.3 billion tiles from 171,189 slides (Nature 2024). In EAGLE's comparison it takes about sixteen minutes per slide.
Rapidly Evolving Agile Laboratory Modules — the family of clinical and research applications built inside Yale Pathology over nearly two decades.
Fetching relevant material at question time and putting it in front of the model, instead of hoping the model memorized it during training.

The corridor of land a route occupies, independent of what runs on it. The Farmington Canal's right-of-way has carried a canal, a railroad, and a bicycle trail; the corridor outlived all three transportation logics.
Running a model prospectively on live cases while hiding its output from the people making decisions. It measures real-world performance without exposing patients to it.
Software as a Medical Device — software that is itself the device. Most pathology AI is not regulated this way, which changes both the evidence expected and the list you find it on.
Turnaround time. At this institution the median has not moved in twenty years — 89 hours in April 2006, 89 hours in April 2026, on 23% more cases.

The Cancer Genome Atlas — the public cohort on which a large share of computational pathology is trained, tuned, and then evaluated. Overlap between those three uses is a stated limitation of the Stanford benchmark.
A small square crop of a whole-slide image, typically 256 pixels at 20×. Models see tiles; pathologists see slides; the gap between those two facts is most of the engineering.
A multimodal whole-slide foundation model (Ding et al., Nat Med 2025). Its mean AUROC over EAGLE's 31 external tasks is 0.740, against EAGLE's 0.742.

A model calling an external function — a search, a script, a database query — and reading the result before continuing. It is the difference between a system that describes an analysis and one that runs it.
A general-purpose pathology foundation model (Chen et al., Nat Med 2024); with UNI2, among the five top-ranked encoders in the Stanford benchmark that cannot be statistically separated.

A 632-million-parameter pathology encoder pre-trained on 3.1 million slides. It is EAGLE's expensive step and the Stanford benchmark's top-ranked model — by a margin the same paper reports as not significant.
The significance test the Stanford benchmark used to compare its top models. Its answer, for the top five, was that there is no difference to report.
Whole-slide image — the digitized glass slide. FDA authorized the first system for primary diagnosis in April 2017.

An open-source synthetic name generator producing linguistically plausible names belonging to no real person — built so that a research pipeline can be tested against realistic, occasionally adversarial, HIPAA-safe data.

slides.title: AI Is Rewriting the Operating System of Pathology
slides.subtitle: A 2026 update on AI in pathology — and why the literature alone cannot supply it

slides.title: Conflict of Interest Disclosure
bullets: Consultant for Applicate Technologies Inc.
This presentation is intended solely for educational purposes. All content reflects the presenter's independent views and does not represent the official position of any institution or vendor.

slides.title: The Brief for This Session
slides.subtitle: A 2026 update on AI in pathology, anchored on two papers the organizers asked to have reviewed

cards.label: The brief
cards.description: Two papers published this year in Nature Communications: an efficiency framework and a 32-model benchmark.

cards.label: What the papers show
cards.description: A two-thousandths AUROC difference in one; 32 models and no statistically separable winner in the other. Both results are correctly reported.

cards.label: What is actually changing
cards.description: Between asking a question, finding data, writing code, running the analysis, publishing, and teaching it.

cards.label: What this session does
cards.description: Not an inventory of what is travelling on the canal — a demonstration that the railroad has arrived, on the canal's own right-of-way.

takeaway.text: The two papers are not outdated. They are conceptually incomplete — and the gap is where the interesting part of 2026 lives.
takeaway.comment: Nothing in this session is a criticism of either paper. Both are excellent and both are correctly reported. The claim is narrower and harder: what changed in 2026 is not measurable on the axis either paper reports. Say “conceptually incomplete”, then move on — the next twenty minutes earns it.

slides.title: Thesis: The Model Stopped Being the Interesting Part
slides.subtitle: The most important pathology-AI development of 2026 may not be a model that reads slides

left.heading: What Has Not Changed
bullets: A glass slide still carries far more information than any single reading extracts
The hard problems are still semantic — what counts as a case, which exception matters, when a formally correct answer is operationally wrong
Discrimination is still not calibration; retrospective performance is still not clinical utility
The pathologist's judgment is still the thing the system cannot supply

right.heading: What Changed
bullets: Choosing a model is ceasing to be the main question — the top five are indistinguishable
The interesting engineering moved to routing, composition, reuse and inspectability
AI systems now use tools: they retrieve, write and run code, query data, and remember
The boundaries between asking, finding, coding, analyzing, publishing and teaching collapsed

takeaway.text: Ten years ago the question was which model. Now the question is what you assemble, what you can inspect, and what you can defend.
takeaway.comment: This is the thesis slide; everything after it is either evidence or consequence. Slow down on the right-hand column's last line — that is the sentence the whole second half of the talk unpacks.

vizConfig.title: Learning objectives
vizConfig.subtitle: Five claims you should be able to make — and defend — by the end of the hour.

objectives.text: Seeing a capability from reproducing it, reproducing it from deploying it, and deploying it from improving outcomes.
A 2026 computational-pathology paper for its engineering lesson, not its headline AUROC.
Why 32 models whose leaders are statistically identical means model choice is no longer the main question.
The frontier across three clocks — capability, engineering, clinical evidence — and the sources that serve each.
What is worth producing: one question whose answer would change a decision, and the artifact that would establish it.

vizConfig.footnote: The progression is deliberate. Objective five is unreachable until the first four are settled, which is why most “AI strategy” conversations stall.

slides.speakerNotes: Read the five verbs, not the five sentences. Distinguish — Read — Explain — Locate — Decide. The last one is the assignment: by the end of the hour, one question in your own practice whose answer would change a decision, and the artifact that would establish it. Not necessarily a paper.

slides.title: Who This Session Is For
slides.subtitle: Look around the room — if any of these describe you, you are exactly the audience
bullets: The pathologist who has now watched four AI demonstrations — and still cannot say what any of them would change about next Thursday's sign-out.
The colleague who read both 2026 papers — and came away with a number, not an idea.
The lab director asked to “have an AI strategy” — by people who mean a purchase order.
The trainee who can already do this — and has never been told that assembling a working system is a legitimate scientific act.
The colleague who suspects this is overhyped — the most valuable person in the room, because the honest version of this argument has to survive that scrutiny.

takeaway.text: If you are any of these, the rest of this session is addressed to you specifically.
takeaway.comment: Look up from the slides. Name the skeptic last and mean it — the talk is stronger if the room believes you have already argued with them in your head.

slides.title: The Two Anchor Papers
slides.subtitle: Both published in Nature Communications in mid-2026. Both excellent. Both bounded in the same direction.

left.heading: EAGLE — Nat Commun 17:5740 (1 Jul 2026)
bullets: Neidlinger, Lenz, Foersch, … Kather
A pipeline: a cheap frozen model ranks ~18,000 tiles; an expensive model re-reads 25
2.27 s of model inference per slide; a single 1,280-dimensional slide embedding
Mean AUROC 0.742 across 31 external tasks, 13 cohorts, 9,528 slides

right.heading: Foundation-model benchmark — Nat Commun 17:9012 (24 Jul 2026)
bullets: Bareja, Carrillo-Perez, … Gevaert (Stanford + Argonne)
32 models, 4 categories, 41 tasks, 53 datasets, more than 17,500 slides
Frozen features, linear probe, mean pooling, 70/30 patient split, 1,000 bootstraps
Top five: 0.830 / 0.829 / 0.824 / 0.824 / 0.824 — and no statistical difference between them

takeaway.text: Do not call them outdated. Call them conceptually incomplete — and then ask what the incompleteness is made of.
takeaway.comment: Name the authors. Colleagues in this room will meet them at USCAP, and the argument only lands if it is visibly respectful. The critique is of what the genre can express, not of the work itself.

vizConfig.title: Route the expensive model. Do not brute-force the slide.
vizConfig.subtitle: Every component here is off the shelf. The contribution is the order they run in — and what is allowed to be expensive.

field.label: EVERY TILE ON ONE SLIDE, AT 2 MICRONS PER PIXEL

vizConfig.fieldNote: About 1,100 tiles at 2 MPP; the same slide is ~18,000 at 0.5 MPP. CTransPath reads every one; CHIEF ranks them.
vizConfig.insetNote: The 25 tiles Virchow2 actually re-reads: about 2% of the tiles at 2 MPP, about 0.1% of the slide at 0.5 MPP.

statements.label: Choosing where to look is the cheapest step here.
One vector per slide, reused by every downstream task.

stations.label: Tessellate
stations.tip: The slide is cut into tiles before any model runs. This step is not in the 2.27 s.

stations.label: CTransPath
stations.tip:
CTransPath, 2.01 s
The cheap pass. It reads everything, at low resolution, once.

stations.label: CHIEF ranks
stations.tip:
CHIEF attention, 0.36 ms
Frozen — no training. Used purely as a ranking function.
Gini of the attention weights: CHIEF 0.702, ABMIL 0.087. Concentration is what makes a ranker.

stations.label: Top 25 tiles
stations.tip: 25 tiles survive. The regions are preserved and can be shown to a pathologist — which is not the same as a faithful causal explanation.

stations.label: Virchow2
stations.tip:
Virchow2, 0.26 s
632 M parameters, pre-trained on 3.1 M slides — pointed at 25 tiles instead of 18,000.

stations.label: Slide embedding
stations.tip: One vector per slide. Cheap to store, cheap to search, reusable across tasks.

vizConfig.hardware: NVIDIA L40 (48 GB) — model inference only
vizConfig.notIncludedLabel: WHAT THAT 2.27 SECONDS DOES NOT INCLUDE
notIncluded: the CTransPath feature cache at 2 MPP
downloading gated weights: Virchow2 by terms acceptance, CHIEF by request
everything a laboratory would call integration
vizConfig.footnote: The repository README reports about three minutes for seven slides on a MacBook Air M3 — which is the more useful number, and it is not in the paper.
vizConfig.source: Neidlinger et al., Nat Commun 17:5740 (2026) · KatherLab/EAGLE

slides.speakerNotes: Walk the rail left to right and land hard on the 0.36 millisecond bar. That sliver is the argument: the step that decides where the expensive model looks costs nothing. This is selective computation and model orchestration — it is closer to systems engineering than to training a better model. Then point at the lower dashed track. The 2.27 seconds is model inference on an L40. It does not include scanning, tiling, the feature cache, weight downloads, or anything a laboratory would recognize as integration. Both facts are true at once, and only one of them is in the abstract.

takeaway.text: The lesson is not the number. It is that a cheap frozen model, used as a router, buys you an expensive model's attention at 2% of the cost.
takeaway.comment: If someone asks whether 25 tiles can miss a rare or dispersed finding: yes, and the authors say so. That is a real limitation, not a rhetorical concession — answer it plainly and move to the honest-reading slide.

vizConfig.title: The interesting number is on the other axis.
vizConfig.subtitle: Mean AUROC over 31 external tasks, against seconds of model inference per slide.

marginal.label: Virchow2 (STAMP) 0.723 — per-slide time not reported here
Prov-GigaPath: about 16 min per slide. Its mean AUROC on this benchmark could not be verified for this review, so it is not plotted.

vizConfig.insetNote: A six-hundredths window. At this magnification the difference is visible — which is exactly the problem.
vizConfig.caption: Mean AUROC across 31 external tasks (13 cohorts, 9,528 WSIs). Seconds are model inference on an NVIDIA L40, not end-to-end. Δ is a difference, not an improvement: the paper reports no significance test for it.
vizConfig.source: EAGLE · Neidlinger et al., Nat Commun 17:5740 (2026)

slides.speakerNotes: Two panels, one point. On the honest axis — 0.50 to 1.00 — EAGLE, TITAN, CONCH and Virchow2 are one dot. Zoom to the window the abstract lives in and a difference appears; that is a property of the zoom, not of the models. Meanwhile the horizontal axis separates them by two orders of magnitude. The interesting part of EAGLE is not two-thousandths over TITAN. It is the transition from brute-force computation to routing, composition, reuse and inspectable execution.

takeaway.text: 0.742 against 0.740 is a difference, not an improvement. 2.27 seconds against 16 minutes is the finding.
takeaway.comment: Never say “improvement” about the delta on this slide. If a statistician in the room presses on it, agree immediately: no significance test is reported for that comparison, and the paper does not claim one.

slides.title: An Honest Reading of a Good Paper

left.heading: What It Shows
bullets: Route cheap to expensive — a frozen ranker decides where the costly model looks
Concentrate compute — 25 tiles instead of 18,000, at about 2% of the tiles at 2 MPP
Reuse — one 1,280-d embedding per slide, stored once, used by every downstream task
Preserve the regions — the 25 tiles survive and can be put in front of a pathologist
Budget as a design objective — speed and cost treated as first-class requirements, not afterthoughts

right.heading: What It Does Not Show
bullets: Inference only, on an L40 — the 2.27 s excludes scanning, tiling, the feature cache and three separate access gates
25 regions can miss a rare or dispersed finding — the authors say so
Sparsity is not explanation — fewer regions are easier to review; that is not a faithful causal account
The pen-mark analysis is 50 slides and one pathologist — pen marks in 16% of EAGLE tiles vs 23% of baseline tiles
Retrospective throughout — the authors write that 0.742 “might not yet be adequate to replace standard clinical procedures”

takeaway.text: Both columns are true. A paper can be excellent, correctly reported, and still unable to answer the question you actually have.
takeaway.comment: The phrase “emulates pathologists” appears around work like this. It emulates selective viewing. Pathologists do many things while looking at a slide; choosing where to look next is one of them, and it is the only one being emulated here.

slides.title: Five Principles, None of Which Are About the Model
slides.subtitle: What a pathology department should actually take from EAGLE

cards.label: Route
cards.description: Let a fast, frozen component decide where the costly component looks. The routing decision cost 0.36 milliseconds.

cards.label: Compose
cards.description: CTransPath, CHIEF and Virchow2 already existed. Nothing was trained. The contribution was the arrangement.

cards.label: Reuse
cards.description: A 1,280-dimensional embedding computed once and reused by every task — storage and search become tractable.

cards.label: Inspect
cards.description: The 25 tiles are preserved and reviewable. Inspectability is a design choice, not a property that emerges.

cards.label: Budget
cards.description: Seconds per slide treated as a first-class objective is what makes the difference between a demo and something a lab can run.

takeaway.text: This is selective computation and model orchestration — closer to AI engineering than to one model doing one task.
takeaway.comment: If your department is going to fund one skill, fund this one. None of these five principles require training a model, and all five require someone who can read a repository.

slides.title: What the Benchmark Actually Did
slides.subtitle: Stanford and Argonne, 32 models, one protocol held constant across all of them

cards.label: Models
cards.description: Four categories: general vision, general vision-language, pathology vision (16 of them), pathology vision-language.

cards.label: Tasks
cards.description: 19 built on TCGA, 22 on non-TCGA data — across 53 datasets and more than 17,500 whole-slide images.

cards.label: Protocol
cards.description: 20×, 256-pixel patches resized to 224, frozen features, linear probe, mean pooling, 70/30 patient-level split.

cards.label: Uncertainty
cards.description: Confidence intervals on every estimate, and Wald tests between the leaders. This is the part that makes the finding a finding.

takeaway.text: A benchmark is a protocol, not a leaderboard. This one held everything constant so that the comparison would mean something.
takeaway.comment: Emphasize the bootstraps. Most leaderboards report a point estimate and let the reader assume the ordering is real. This one measured whether the ordering is real, and then reported that it is not.

vizConfig.title: Thirty-two models later, the result is not a winner.
vizConfig.subtitle: Top five encoders on the 19 TCGA tasks. Whiskers are 95% confidence intervals.
vizConfig.band: NO STATISTICAL DIFFERENCE AMONG THESE FIVE (WALD TESTS)

models.hover:
Virchow2
632 M parameters
3.1 M pre-training slides
Hugging Face: gated

Prov-GigaPath
171,189 slides / 1.3 B tiles
parameter count: could not be verified for this review

H-optimus-0
Bioptimus, 2024
parameters and pre-training scale: could not be verified for this review

UNI
Chen et al., Nat Med 2024
scale figures: could not be verified for this review

UNI2
2025
scale figures: could not be verified for this review

vizConfig.factorsLabel: WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY CHANGE THE RANKING
vizConfig.caption: Frozen features and a linear probe, mean pooling, 70/30 patient-level split, 1,000 bootstraps, 4×A100. On patch-level tasks Virchow2 does separate from the rest (FDR p<0.001) — the saturation claim is about slide-level ranking.
vizConfig.source: Bareja et al., Nat Commun 17:9012 (2026) · gevaertlab/benchmarking-path-models

slides.speakerNotes: The band across the confidence intervals is the finding. Thirty-two models, and the top five cannot be separated by a Wald test. Read the right-hand column slowly — those ten factors are where the variance actually went. Every one of them is an institutional decision, not a download. And note the honest exception in the caption: at patch level Virchow2 does separate. The saturation claim is about slide-level ranking, and I will not overstate it.

takeaway.text: The result is not that a model won. The result is that choosing a model is ceasing to be the main question.
takeaway.comment: This is the slide that reframes the procurement conversation. If the model is not the differentiator, the integration is — and integration is a local capability, which is what makes an applied informatics team fundable.

vizConfig.title: Scaling stopped being the lever.
vizConfig.subtitle: And ensembling the top five does not rescue it either.

bars.label: Majority-vote fusion of the top five

vizConfig.barsNote: Six thousandths apart, with standard deviations of eleven and ten hundredths. The paper reports the difference as not significant at task level — and on non-TCGA tasks Virchow2 alone (0.712) is ahead of the fusion (0.699).
vizConfig.finding: neither increasing model size nor pre-training dataset size uniformly guarantees improved performance

binGroups.label: MODEL-SIZE BINS USED IN THE ANALYSIS

vizConfig.closing: No per-model scatter is drawn here: the per-model parameter counts could not be verified for this review. Drawing a cloud of plausible points would be exactly the failure this slide is about.

slides.speakerNotes: Two claims. First: the ensemble does not save you. Fusing the top five gives 0.702 against 0.696 for Virchow2 alone, with standard deviations that swamp the difference, and on non-TCGA data the single model is actually ahead. Second: the scaling story, quoted verbatim. Neither more parameters nor more pre-training slides uniformly helps. Point at the closing note if anyone asks why there is no scatter plot — I did not have verified per-model parameter counts, so I did not draw one. Optional slide; cut it first if the demos are running long.

slides.title: What a Benchmark Cannot See
slides.subtitle: Four limitations the authors state, and five that are outside the design by construction

left.heading: Stated by the Authors
bullets: Frozen features and linear probing — a lower bound, not a ceiling
Possible pre-training / evaluation overlap — TCGA and CPTAC appear on both sides
Coarse scaling proxies — parameter and data bins are blunt instruments
Simple mean pooling — almost certainly leaving performance unmeasured
And separately: in ten public foundation models, the medical center of origin is predicted more accurately than the tissue type (de Jong et al., 2025)

right.heading: Outside the Design Entirely
bullets: Calibration — not evaluated. This is an observation of the present review, not a limitation the authors state
Decision curves — no net-benefit analysis at any threshold
Prospective workflow effects — no measurement of what changes when the tool is actually used
Comparison against pathologists — not part of the protocol
Patient outcomes — not in scope here, and rarely in scope anywhere in this literature

takeaway.text: The benchmark's code, dashboard, dependencies and reproducibility may tell us as much about the state of the field as its AUROC tables do.
takeaway.comment: Be scrupulous here. The word “calibration” does not appear in the paper; the observation belongs to this review, and the authors should not be credited with a limitation they did not state. That distinction is the ethic of the whole session.

slides.title: Poll: Where Does Your Sense of the Field Come From?
slides.prompt: Where do you actually get your sense of what AI can do in pathology today?
slides.note: We will come back to your answers when we look at what each kind of artifact can and cannot establish.

vizConfig.title: The boundaries collapsed. The judgment did not.
vizConfig.subtitle: Eight activities that used to require a different person, a different budget line, and usually a different building.
vizConfig.hub: one tool-using, code-writing, retrieving, remembering system

activities.label: Ask the question
activities.artifact: Still yours. This is one of the two things the ring cannot supply.

activities.label: Find the data
activities.artifact: Retrieval and connectors — though there is still no pathology connector in Claude for Life Sciences (Oct 2025).

activities.label: Write the code
activities.artifact: NOVA (Nov 2025) writes and runs Python across 49 tools.

activities.label: Run the analysis
activities.artifact: TissueLab orchestrates local tools and co-evolves with use (Sep 2025).

activities.label: Navigate the slide
activities.artifact: PathAgent — Navigator, Perceptor, Executor (Nov 2025); PathNavigate budgets the search (May 2026).

activities.label: Visualize and explain
activities.artifact: Pathology-CoT learns from recorded expert viewer behaviour (Oct 2025).

activities.label: Publish it
activities.artifact: The bottleneck moved: 992 pathology-AI papers by September 2026 alone.

activities.label: Teach it
activities.artifact: This deck. One JSON file, editable during the questions.

vizConfig.humanNote: The human is not removed from the loop. They move to the two inputs the loop cannot generate for itself.
vizConfig.caption: Nothing in the ring was deleted. Every activity still happens — but the handoff between them stopped costing a grant cycle.

slides.speakerNotes: Left side first: eight activities, and between each pair a crimson bar. That bar is the handoff, and the handoff is what cost money and time. A grant. A collaborator. A journal. A reviewer. A course. Then watch the bars fade. On the right the same eight activities sit on one ring around a system that uses tools. Hover any of them during questions — each one has a 2025 or 2026 pathology artifact behind it. And note where the human is: outside the ring, holding the question and the judgment. That is not a consolation prize. Those are the two scarce inputs, and this whole talk is an argument about how to spend them.

takeaway.text: The collapse is not that the work disappeared. It is that the handoffs between the pieces of work stopped costing a grant cycle.
takeaway.comment: If someone objects that this is hype: ask them which of the eight boxes still requires a different person in their own department. Usually two or three, and the number is falling. That is the honest version of the claim.

slides.title: What “AI” Now Means, When It Is Not a Slide Classifier
slides.subtitle: The capability set the two anchor papers do not measure — and are not trying to

cards.label: Agentic Coding
cards.description: A loop that proposes a change, runs it, reads the failure, tries again — with a human owning the spec and the merge.

cards.label: Tool Use
cards.value: It Calls, It Reads, It Continues
cards.description: MCP turned one-integration-per-pair into one interface. There is still no pathology connector.

cards.label: Retrieval and Memory
cards.description: What the system has in front of it at each step. This has replaced prompt wording as what decides whether it works.

cards.label: Continuous Evaluation
cards.description: Regression suites for behaviour, not just code — plus monitoring for the day the scanner or case mix changes.

cards.label: The Boundary
cards.description: No autonomous diagnosis. No PHI in prompts. No hidden transformations. No unverified production code.

takeaway.text: Five capabilities, one of which is a prohibition. The prohibition is what makes the other four deployable in a regulated laboratory.
takeaway.comment: Read the last card aloud, in full. A research audience hearing the AI argument for the first time needs to hear the boundary stated as firmly as the capability. Every risk here has a testable mitigation: hallucinated logic goes to unit tests, prompt drift to regression suites, leakage to a structurally enforced no-PHI policy.

slides.dockTitle: The pathology agent became a genre

vizConfig.title: In two years the pathology agent became a genre.
vizConfig.subtitle: Systems, the plumbing they run on, and the evidence about whether any of it helps. Hover for detail; click to open the source.

vizConfig.caption: The two copper diamonds are the anchor papers. They sit at the far right of the evidence lane — after almost every capability event above them. That is not a criticism of the authors; it is what peer review costs.
vizConfig.source: Full citations on the sources slide

slides.speakerNotes: Do not read this timeline out. Let the room look at the shape of it. Top lane: eleven systems in twenty-four months, almost all of them preprints. Middle lane: the plumbing, and one deliberate red mark — Claude for Life Sciences shipped connectors for Benchling, PubMed and Synapse in October 2025, and there is still no connector for a pathology archive. Bottom lane: the evidence, sparse, and the two anchor papers arriving last. Also in crimson: a twenty-eight-author expert review in March 2026 whose finding is that real-world adoption has lagged. I am putting that on the slide because a timeline that only goes one direction is propaganda.

takeaway.text: Capability moves in preprints and repositories. Evidence moves in journals. Reading only the second and calling it the state of the field is a category error.
takeaway.comment: The counterweight matters. Twenty-eight authors, March 2026: real-world adoption has lagged. Both things are true — the genre expanded rapidly and almost none of it is in routine laboratory use. That tension is the honest position.

slides.title: Two Kinds of System, Both Necessary

left.heading: What the LIS Does — and Must Keep Doing
bullets: Moves predefined records through predefined channels
“The system recorded it” — accession, result, report, release
Metrics after the fact: turnaround-time reports, volumes, backlogs
Every case in the building depends on it, and will for years
Necessary. Not designed to help you construct a route that does not exist yet.

right.heading: What the Emerging Systems Do
bullets: Help construct the route while the work is under way
Route work, surface exceptions, coordinate handoffs, adapt to what actually happened
Treat the question as something to sharpen, not as a fixed input
Produce artifacts — code, embeddings, evaluations — that outlive the question that prompted them
Insufficient on their own. Nothing here replaces the record of what was done.

takeaway.text: This is not LIS versus AI. It is a system that records a route against a system that helps you build one — and a laboratory needs both.
takeaway.comment: Do not let this become a vendor-bashing slide. Epic, Beaker, and every LIS in the room are doing exactly what they were built to do. The failure is expecting the record-keeping layer to also be the orchestration layer. It never was.

vizConfig.title: Three clocks — and we keep reading the slowest one as if it were the fastest.
vizConfig.subtitle: Click a face: the other two dim, and that clock's 2026 example appears.

clocks.name: Capability
clocks.question: What can be done today?
clocks.example: Nov 2025: NOVA writes and runs Python across 49 tools. Nov 2025: PathAgent navigates a slide. Both preprints.

clocks.name: Engineering
clocks.question: Can it be made reliable, reproducible, economical and safe?
clocks.example: 2025 DICOM WSI Connectathon: 32 implementers. IHE DPIA: still Trial Implementation. EAGLE: three separate access gates before you can run it.

clocks.name: Clinical evidence
clocks.question: Does it improve clinical work or patient care, under a defined intended use?
clocks.example: Articulate Pro: 1,613 prospective cases, diagnosis or grade group changed in 5.4%, management-relevant in 1.3%, turnaround time down 30.1 hours at one site.

pointer.read: and we read it as a description of this one

vizConfig.caption: The hands are running at 1 : 1/8 : 1/60. In the two minutes we spend on this slide, the capability hand will lap the evidence hand roughly twenty times.

slides.speakerNotes: Let the clocks run for a beat before saying anything. Three clocks, three different questions, three different literatures. The mistake almost everybody makes — me included — is reading a journal article, which serves the slow clock, as if it described the fast one. A paper accepted in June 2026 describes work done in 2024 and 2025. That is not a flaw in journals; that is what peer review costs. The fix is not to stop reading journals. It is to learn to read repositories, model cards, issue trackers, standards documents and regulatory records as evidence too — each for the one thing it can establish.

vizConfig.title: Seeing it is not reproducing it. Reproducing it is not deploying it.
vizConfig.subtitle: Four claims, four kinds of evidence. We routinely accept the first as proof of the fourth.

rungs.evidence: EAGLE: 2.27 s per slide, mean AUROC 0.742 over 31 external tasks. Retrospective, all cohorts.
The README: about 3 minutes for 7 slides on a MacBook Air M3 — after clearing three access gates. Across computational pathology, few published algorithms are reused.
rungs.source: KatherLab/EAGLE · Wagner et al., Mod Pathol 2024

rungs.claim: It survives contact with a workflow
rungs.evidence: Articulate Pro: 1,613 cases, 1,049 AI-assisted; diagnosis or grade group changed in 21 of 386 (5.4%); management-relevant in 5 (1.3%); TAT down 30.1 h at one site; IHC odds ratios 0.50, 0.43, 0.33.
No pathology-AI study with a patient-outcome endpoint was identified for this review. Corrections are welcome during discussion — and this rung can be filled in on the spot.

verbs.detail: LIS, viewer, HL7, an intended use

vizConfig.caption: Each gap has a verb, and each verb is where a project dies. Most pathology-AI conversations are conducted entirely on rung one.

slides.speakerNotes: Four rungs. The fourth is dashed and empty, and it stays empty: no pathology-AI study with a patient-outcome endpoint was identified for this review. If anyone in the room knows of one, that is the most useful thing that can come out of the discussion, and the deck can be corrected before the session ends — which, given how it is built, is a literal statement. Note the verbs between the rungs: install, integrate, measure. Every one of them is an institutional capability, not a download.

vizConfig.title: 1,524 AI-enabled devices are authorized. Nine of them are pathology.
vizConfig.subtitle: FDA AI-enabled medical devices by lead review panel — the slowest clock, rendered as a list.
vizConfig.yearsNote: 2026 is partial — through 30 March. 2025 was a record year across all panels.
vizConfig.entriesLabel: THE NINE PATHOLOGY ENTRIES, ON A TIME AXIS
vizConfig.modernNote: Four of the nine are whole-slide-image algorithms: Paige 2021, Hologic 2024, Ibex 2025, Artera 2025. Pathology AI is generally reviewed as an IVD component under OHT7, not as software-as-a-medical-device — which is part of why this list is short.
vizConfig.disclaimer: FDA's own caveat, verbatim: “The list is not a comprehensive resource of AI-enabled medical devices.” List page dated 16 June 2026; table parsed 2 September 2026.
vizConfig.source: FDA AI-Enabled Medical Devices list · Innolitics 2026 snapshot: 51 AI/ML devices in pathology-adjacent panels, 7 of them WSI algorithms

slides.speakerNotes: Radiology has 1,164. Pathology has nine, and four of them are whole-slide-image algorithms. The right-hand time axis has the last two entries offset so the labels do not collide — the dates in the hover are the real ones. Two honest caveats. First, the FDA says on its own page that this list is not comprehensive, and I am putting that sentence on the slide rather than in my mouth. Second, the reason the number is small is partly structural: pathology AI is reviewed as an IVD, not as SaMD, so it does not all land on this list. The shape is still the point — the regulatory clock is the slow one, and it is where an intended use gets defined.

LIVE DEMO ONE. The top half is what the investigator does: asks a natural-language question, gets a cohort back in seconds instead of weeks. The bottom half is the part this room needs to see clearly — IBIS was built outside the institution, on entirely synthetic data, in a Docker-based Elasticsearch stack that has never touched PHI. The pathway in is the responsible one: open source, adapt to the internal data model, Enterprise GitHub, security review, CI/CD. If the live instance is up, run two queries now. One structured — cohort by IHC profile or stage. One free-text — a concept with no code behind it. After each: one short sentence. “Notice, no SQL was written.” “Notice, that came out of a free-text report, not a coded field.” If the demo is unavailable, switch to the recorded fallback and do not apologize. The talk works without it; it does not work without the idea of it.

takeaway.text: No SQL was written, and nothing here has ever touched PHI. Both of those are engineering decisions, not luck.
takeaway.comment: This is the existence proof for the whole second half of the talk. One informaticist, synthetic data, an applied team for the safety review. The methodology existed before AI; what changed was the cost of building, which is what made it feasible at that scale.

slides.title: Xenonym — A Tool That Was Never Worth Building Before
slides.subtitle: Live at xenonym.openpathology.org — a sixty-second demonstration

takeaway.text: Synthetic names that sound like names, belong to nobody, and include the ones that break your pipeline.
takeaway.comment: Bobby Tables is not a joke, it is a test case. If your research pipeline cannot store “Nontra Null” or “Čapek”, that is a bug, and depending on context a compliance failure waiting to happen. The point is not the tool. The point is that supplementary infrastructure of this size is now affordable to build — which is the same economic claim the rest of the talk makes about bigger things.

slides.speakerNotes: LIVE DEMO TWO. Press D for the full dashboard; ESC closes it. April 2006 against April 2026 at this institution. Twenty-three percent more cases. Every digital tool the field produced in between. Mean turnaround time went from 101 hours to 106. Median went from 89 to 89. The share signed out within two days fell slightly. This is the bridge to the closing metaphor: the canal carried more boats every year, and it never got faster. The tools were real. The orchestration layer that would have turned those tools into shorter cycle times was never built.

takeaway.text: Twenty years of tools, 23% more cases, and a median turnaround time of 89 hours in both April 2006 and April 2026.
takeaway.comment: Do not let this land as cynicism. The right reading is diagnostic: we bought capability and never built the layer that converts capability into cycle time. That layer is the subject of the last third of this talk.

vizConfig.title: The mirror: what happens when producing an academically legible object gets cheap.
vizConfig.subtitle: PubMed records per year. The 2026 bars are partial — through 2 September.

marginalia.text: of 2024 biomedical abstracts show signs of LLM processing — a lower bound, measured on abstracts.
marginalia.source: KOBAK ET AL., SCI ADV 11(27) 2025 · >15 M ABSTRACTS

marginalia.text: of 2025 papers show excess LLM-associated vocabulary — measured on full text. A different measure from the one above; do not read them as a trend line.

vizConfig.footnote: 70% of 5,114 journals now have an AI-use policy. Measured across 5.2 million papers, the policies made no significant difference to usage (He & Bu, 2025).
vizConfig.caption: This slide is not an accusation. Volume was rising before LLMs — 47% more articles between 2016 and 2022. What AI did was collapse the cost of producing an object that looks like a contribution, and thereby expose how much of the existing corpus already was one.
vizConfig.source: PubMed E-utilities counts, run 2 September 2026; query strings in the lecture repository

slides.speakerNotes: Two series and two numbers in the margin, deliberately kept off the axis because they measure different things. Thirteen and a half percent is a lower bound on 2024 abstracts. Eighty-nine percent is full-text vocabulary in 2025 papers. Plotting those together as a trend would be exactly the kind of compression this talk is complaining about. And the footnote is the finding that should worry a journal editor: seventy percent of journals have a policy, and the policies changed nothing measurable. Now the hard sentence, and I want to say it carefully. This is not an accusation about anyone's writing. Never infer authorship from style. The claim is systemic: AI exposes the enormous volume of academically legible but low-marginal-value production inside science, including in our field.

takeaway.text: AI did not create low-value science. It collapsed the cost of producing the thing that looks like science, and thereby exposed how much of it there already was.
takeaway.comment: Guardrail, hold it firmly: never infer AI authorship from writing style. The claim on this slide is about the system, not about any individual paper or author. If a question pushes toward naming names, refuse it and restate the systemic version.

slides.dockTitle: What got cheap, what stayed scarce

vizConfig.title: What got cheap, and what did not.
vizConfig.subtitle: Nothing on the right became more abundant. It only became more decisive.
vizConfig.closing: If AI makes it almost effortless to produce papers, code, analyses and presentations, then our responsibility is no longer to produce more. It is to decide what is worth producing, how it should be tested, and whether it changes anything that matters.
vizConfig.caution: Was that corpus “produced using AI”? In a systemic sense, increasingly yes — whether or not a model wrote any given sentence. Authorship must never be inferred from writing style.

slides.speakerNotes: Let the left column visibly lose weight while you say nothing. Then read four items from the right column slowly. Every one of them is a human institutional capability, and not one of them has a vendor. Close on the sentence at the bottom — it is the thesis of the last act, and it is the sentence I want the room to leave with.

vizConfig.title: Every artifact answers exactly one question well.
vizConfig.subtitle: We spent thirty years asking the paper to answer all nine. Hover a row for its 2026 example.

artifacts.label: Peer-reviewed paper
artifacts.example: EAGLE, Nat Commun 17:5740. It records a claim and its formal evidence — and that is what it is for.

artifacts.label: Video or demo
artifacts.example: A NOVA or PathChat walkthrough. It transmits tacit knowledge that no methods section can.

artifacts.label: Repository
artifacts.example: KatherLab/EAGLE, GPL-3.0, Zenodo-archived. It shows the method runs — and its issues reveal where it does not.

artifacts.label: Model card
artifacts.example: paige-ai/Virchow2 on Hugging Face, gated. It states what the model was trained on and what it is not for.

artifacts.label: Issue tracker
artifacts.example: The only artifact in this list whose primary job is to surface failure modes.

artifacts.label: Interactive benchmark
artifacts.example: pathbench.stanford.edu. It lets a comparison stay live after the paper is frozen.

artifacts.label: Regulatory record
artifacts.example: Paige Prostate, DEN200080. It is the only artifact here that defines an approved intended use.

artifacts.label: Prospective implementation
artifacts.example: Articulate Pro: 1,613 cases, and a measurement of what changed in the reporting workflow.

artifacts.label: Clinical-outcomes study
artifacts.example: None was identified in pathology AI for this review. The row is aspirational.

vizConfig.overclaimLabel: WHAT WE HAVE BEEN ASKING THE PAPER TO DO
vizConfig.closing: Views measure attention. Peer review measures passage through a validation process. Neither of them directly measures clinical usefulness — and a field that conflates the three will keep being surprised.

slides.speakerNotes: This is the slide to return to the poll on. Whatever the room answered — journals, preprints, vendor demos, YouTube, colleagues, trying it yourself — none of those answers is wrong. Each of them is a row in this matrix, and each row establishes exactly one thing. The failure is not using YouTube. The failure is treating a demo as evidence of deployment, or a paper as evidence of outcome. Watch the copper rings appear across the paper row: that is what academic culture has been asking one artifact to do on its own. Read the closing line as written.

slides.dockTitle: From the memex to the model

vizConfig.title: Bush described the trail. We finally built something that can walk one.
vizConfig.subtitle: Eighty years from the memex to a system that constructs the trail while you are still asking the question.

events.label: Bush, “As We May Think”
events.tip: The memex: stores, extends, and above all lets you consult trails.

events.label: Knuth, “Literate Programming”
events.tip: A program written as an explanation to a human being, with the code embedded in the prose.

events.label: Model Context Protocol
events.tip: One interface between models and tools, instead of one integration per pair.

quotes: A record if it is to be useful to science, must be continuously extended, it must be stored, and above all it must be consulted.
The process of tying two items together is the important thing.
There is a new profession of trail blazers.
vizConfig.additionsLabel: WHAT THE MODEL ADDS TO THE MEMEX
additions: It constructs the trail, not only stores it
It writes and runs the code
It proposes connections you did not ask for
It regenerates the explanation for a new audience
It preserves the process, not just the result
And it will confidently invent a trail that is not there

slides.speakerNotes: Bush wanted a machine that stores, extends and consults — and he understood that the intellectual act was the trail, not the storage. Read the third quote: “There is a new profession of trail blazers.” He was describing a job that did not exist. It exists now, and some of you already have it. The right-hand list is what the model adds to the memex. Read the last item aloud with the same weight as the others: it will confidently invent a trail that is not there. That item is on the slide on purpose. An honest list of new capabilities includes the new failure mode.

vizConfig.title: This deck is the argument, not a picture of it.
vizConfig.subtitle: There is no PowerPoint here. One JSON file, a D3 visualization library, a test suite, and a commit hash.

vizConfig.loopLabel: a question from the room re-enters at step one
vizConfig.caption: The medium demonstrates the argument. If a question in this session exposes something the deck answers badly, the fix is a pull request — not a reprint.

slides.speakerNotes: Twenty minutes ago I claimed that the boundaries between asking, finding, coding, analyzing, publishing and teaching have collapsed. This slide is the receipt. A brief, three research passes, a registry where every number carries a source and a verification status, sixteen visualization specs, a coding agent, and three test gates. Then the loop: a question from this room re-enters at step one. That is not a metaphor. Six of the numbers in this deck are marked TODO in the registry and are deliberately not rendered anywhere — including one AUROC I would have liked to show you on the compute slide. The registry says I did not verify it, so the slide says so too.

vizConfig.title: The canal was necessary, expensive, and obsolete within twenty years.
vizConfig.subtitle: The railroad did not go around it. It was laid on the canal's own right-of-way — and the bike path is on it now.

top.label: NEW HAVEN TO NORTHAMPTON — ONE CORRIDOR, THREE TRANSPORTATION LOGICS

events.label: Groundbreaking — the governor's ceremonial shovel broke
events.tip: 4 July 1825, Granby. Chartered 1822 under James Hillhouse, treasurer of Yale.

events.label: Open to Northampton — about 80 miles, 60 locks
Shareholders lose more than $1 million

bottom.label: PATHOLOGY INFRASTRUCTURE — AND WHAT IS BEING LAID ON TOP OF IT

segments.label: LIS · HL7 · DICOM — STILL CARRYING EVERY CASE

events.label: DICOM Supplement 145 (WSI) — final text
events.tip: Sixteen years old. The 2025 Connectathon counted 32 implementers; IHE DPIA is still Trial Implementation.

Paige Prostate — first FDA de novo AI in pathology
Foundation models: UNI, CONCH, Prov-GigaPath, CHIEF, Virchow2
Agents become a genre; two anchor papers land

vizConfig.marginalia: Toll revenue covered about 20% of expenses. The canal turned a profit once in its first ten years, and cost its shareholders more than a million dollars — and it was still the right thing to have built, because it proved the corridor.
vizConfig.yaleNote: The canal's first president was James Hillhouse, treasurer of Yale. The man who converted it to a railroad, Joseph E. Sheffield, endowed the Sheffield Scientific School — the institution's answer to where applied knowledge belongs.
vizConfig.closing: My goal is not to give you an inventory of everything travelling on the canal. My goal is to show you that the railroad has arrived — and that it is running on the canal's right-of-way, not around it.

slides.speakerNotes: Top band: the Farmington Canal, which ran two hundred yards from where some of you parked. Chartered by Yale's treasurer. The governor's shovel broke at the groundbreaking, which is the most honest omen in the history of infrastructure. It reached Northampton in 1835 with sixty locks, lost over a million dollars, and closed on the eighteenth of January 1848 — the same day the railroad opened on its right-of-way. The tracks had been laid alongside the working canal the year before. In 1996 the corridor became a bike trail. Three transportation logics, one right-of-way. Bottom band: our own corridor. DICOM WSI in 2010. FDA in 2017. Paige in 2021. Then, from 2024, the iron overlay begins — and note that the rail is drawn only to today and ends in an arrowhead. The railroad has arrived. It is not finished. And the canal is not closing: the LIS carries every case in this building and will keep doing so for years. What changed is the transportation logic.

slides.title: Your Move

epigraph.text: You do not need to build models. You need to be the person who knows which question would change a decision.

steps.question: Name the question
steps.detail: One question in your own practice whose answer would change a decision.

steps.question: Name the artifact
steps.detail: A paper, a repository, a model card, a silent trial, a prospective evaluation?

steps.question: Find the rung
steps.detail: Saw it, reproduced it, deployed it, improved outcomes — where does yours sit?

steps.question: Read one repository
steps.detail: Not a paper. One repository: README, issues, licence, access gates.

steps.question: Bring it to the team
steps.detail: The applied informatics team — or the first informaticist who could become one.

takeaway.text: One question, one artifact, one rung, one repository, one conversation.
takeaway.comment: The bottleneck is no longer implementation. It is deciding what is worth implementing — and that is the thing you are uniquely qualified to do.

slides.speakerNotes: Five moves on a commitment timeline. Today: name the question. This week: name the artifact that would establish it. This month: locate it honestly on the evidence ladder. This quarter: read one repository end to end — README, issues, licence, access gates — because thirty minutes there tells you more about whether a thing is deployable than the abstract ever will. This year: take it to the people who can build it. Make each step sound small, because each one is. The compound effect is what changes a department.

takeaway.text: One question, one artifact, one rung, one repository, one conversation.
takeaway.comment: The bottleneck is no longer implementation. It is deciding what is worth implementing — and that is the thing you are uniquely qualified to do.

slides.title: Key Takeaways
items: EAGLE's lesson is orchestration — route, compose, reuse, inspect, budget — not two-thousandths of AUROC. A cheap frozen model bought an expensive one's attention at 2% of the cost.
Thirty-two models later there is no winner, and that is the finding. Data composition, task definition, evaluation design, calibration and integration now matter more than model identity.

The frontier runs on three clocks. The literature serves the slowest and is read as the fastest. Learn to read repositories, model cards, issue trackers, standards and regulatory records as evidence — each for the one thing it can establish.

AI collapsed the cost of academically legible output and thereby exposed how much of it was low-marginal-value. The scarce resources are questions, data, judgment, evaluation, integration, accountability and trusted attention.
The railroad has arrived. The LIS canal still carries every case and will for years. What changed is not the corridor — it is the transportation logic running on it.

cta.label: Your challenge:
cta.text: Write down one question in your practice whose answer would change a decision. Name the artifact that would establish it — and if the honest answer is “a prospective evaluation in my own laboratory” rather than “a paper”, say so, and bring it to your applied informatics team. If your institution does not have such a team, that single page is the strongest case you can make for funding one.

slides.subtitle: What is the one question in your practice whose answer would change a decision — and what artifact, not necessarily a paper, would establish it?
slides.contact:
Peter Gershkovich, MD. MHA
Director of Pathology Informatics & Cancer Data Science
Yale University School of Medicine

A question to open the discussion:
“What is the one question in your practice whose answer would change a decision — and what artifact, not necessarily a paper, would establish it?”

And one this review could not answer:
“Is there a pathology-AI study with a patient-outcome endpoint? The fourth rung is still empty.”

slides.speakerNotes: Optional slide, for audiences that have not seen the OneIT talk. Tufte published The Cognitive Style of PowerPoint in 2003 and was right about all of it, and nothing changed for twenty years — because he never gave anyone anywhere to go. The switching cost stayed at ninety-five. What changed in 2023 was not the argument. It was the price of leaving.
